title: What If Insects Were the Size of Dogs?

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine: The History of Air
Argonne Advanced Photon Source: What Keeps Bugs from Being Bigger? (Kaiser et al. 2007, PNAS)
ASU Ask A Biologist: Prehistoric Insects and Giant Bugs
Clapham & Karr 2012, PNAS: Environmental and biotic controls on the evolutionary history of insect body size
National Geographic: Giant Bugs Eaten Out of Existence by First Birds?

scenes.narration: Imagine a beetle as big as a golden retriever, strolling past you on the sidewalk.
Hit like if that gave you chills.
It's not pure fantasy. About three hundred million years ago, a dragonfly relative called Meganeura had wings spanning almost seventy centimeters.
Back then, the air may have held as much as thirty-five percent oxygen. Today, it's twenty-one.
That matters, because insects have no lungs. Air seeps through a network of tiny tubes, and the bigger the bug, the farther it has to travel.
X-ray studies of living beetles found the tubes into their legs are the bottleneck. The math predicts a limit matching today's biggest beetle, the Titan beetle.
So in today's air, a dog-sized beetle would probably struggle to get oxygen to its legs.
But there's a twist. One study found insect size tracked oxygen for about a hundred fifty million years, until birds appeared. After that, insects shrank, even as oxygen rose.
So the reason you'll never meet a dog-sized bug might be flying right over your head.

claims.claim: Meganeura had a wingspan of almost 70 cm, about 300 million years ago in the Late Carboniferous
Oxygen may have reached as high as 35 percent of the atmosphere in the Late Carboniferous, versus about 21 percent today
Insects breathe through tracheal tubes rather than lungs; as insects get bigger the distance air must travel increases

X-ray imaging of living beetles found larger beetles invest proportionally more in tracheae; the constriction of tracheae leading to the legs predicts a maximum size matching the largest living beetle, Titanus giganteus
Maximum insect size tracked atmospheric oxygen for about 150 million years until birds evolved; afterwards insect size decreased even as oxygen rose
Researchers proposed that agile birds hunting insects limited insect size

meta.summary: 300 million years ago, dragonfly relatives had wings nearly 70 cm across. Here's why today's air keeps bugs small, and the surprising role birds may have played.
